title: The butter thief
hook: the God who holds every world gets caught with butter on his hands, and his mother loves him anyway
carry: vatsalya: loving god like your own child

segments.voice: Yesterday: rakhi, a thread on a brother's wrist and a promise of protection. Your line was raksha, protecting your people is dharma. Today, the midnight birthday again.

Same birthday, other side of the door: the kitchen. For many Hindu families, Janmashtami isn't only a story told. It's a day cooked, sung and stayed up for. And the morning after, in Maharashtra, young men climb on each other's shoulders, level on level, to reach a clay pot of yogurt hanging over the street.
screen: `THE SAME NIGHT, FROM THE KITCHEN.` → `A DAY COOKED, SUNG, STAYED UP FOR.` → `A HUMAN TOWER AND A POT.`

segments.voice: The day begins with a fast. Some take no food at all, some only fruit and milk, until midnight. A small cradle, a jhula, is set up for baby Krishna, and people sing bhajans, devotional songs. At twelve the conch sounds, and the little image is bathed in milk and honey, dressed in tiny new clothes, and rocked. Only then is the fast broken, often with sweets made of milk and butter. Why butter? Because of the child. In the Bhagavata Purana, Krishna grows up among cowherds in Gokul, and the women come to his mother, Yashoda, to complain: he steals our butter, he feeds it to the monkeys, he breaks the pots. They hang the pots high; he piles up stools and mortars and climbs. Then the same chapter tells something astonishing. The boys report that Krishna has eaten dirt. Yashoda makes him open his mouth, and inside it she sees the whole universe: sky, mountains, oceans, stars, even her own village, and herself. She's shaken. And then, the Bhagavata says, the Lord lets her forget, and she simply picks up her boy and loves him. That's the teaching. Hindus call it vatsalya: loving God the way a parent loves a child. The God who holds every world chose to be scolded, fed and rocked to sleep. It's why many families keep a small image of baby Krishna, Laddu Gopal, and care for him every day: bathe him, dress him, feed him. And it's why, the day after, in Maharashtra, teams called govindas build human towers to break a pot of yogurt, Dahi Handi, cheering for the butter thief.
screen: `THE CRADLE, THE CONCH, THE BATH.` · `MAKHAN CHOR: THE BUTTER THIEF.` · `THE UNIVERSE IN HIS MOUTH.` · then, large: `VATSALYA: LOVING GOD LIKE YOUR OWN CHILD.` · `LADDU GOPAL AND DAHI HANDI.`

segments.voice: Many families tend baby Krishna like a child of the house. For the sit, picture him in his cradle with butter on his hands, or a small child you love. Feel how that love asks nothing back. On each slow breath out, say softly, Gopala, little cowherd, or if you don't pray, just rest in that tenderness. Let it be warm, not solemn.
Janmashtami. Krishna's birthday: a fast, a cradle rocked at midnight, and a God loved like a child, the butter thief.
Your line: vatsalya, loving God like your own child. Yashoda saw the universe, then picked him up anyway. That's day six hundred seventy-seven.

howItsDone: Many Hindus fast on Janmashtami, sing bhajans, bathe and dress an image of baby Krishna at midnight and rock it in a cradle, then break the fast with milk sweets; many families keep a Laddu Gopal image and care for him daily, and in Maharashtra Dahi Handi teams build human pyramids the next day.

fork.setup: you're Yashoda. you've just seen the whole universe inside your little boy's mouth. what happens next, in the Bhagavata?

fork.reveal: the Lord lets her forget, and her love as a mother goes on. that's vatsalya, the love many Hindus offer baby Krishna.

original.note: Hindi mākhan (butter) + cor (thief): an affectionate name for the child Krishna.

what a scholar hears: the Bhagavata's tenth book (10.8) sets the butter theft beside the universe in Krishna's mouth; vatsalya as a named mood of devotion is developed in later Vaishnava teaching, notably the Gaudiya school.
